column1: # What each reading, table and curve means, in plain words: id<TAB>meaning. The reading's own label names
# it; this says what it tells you about the sound and when it matters. Every reading, table or curve id in
# the listener's source has a row, and every row an id the source holds (tests/glossary.rs).
# Numbers that belong to a definition (a band, a window) live in the reading's label and source.

column2: How big the very first sample is against the peak. A sound that starts with a jump rather than rising from zero clicks.
How long the sound takes from its onset to its loudest sample. Short for a hard stick on a tight head, long for a soft mallet or a slow swell.
Which way the first half-cycle goes: up (+1) or down (−1). Two otherwise equal hits of opposite polarity can sound different when layered or mixed with a room.
How loud each early window is against the sound's peak: the shape of the first milliseconds.
How bright the attack is: where the energy of the first moments sits (its spectral centroid). Higher means a clickier, harder strike.
The frequency under which 85 % of the attack's power lies: how far up the strike's energy reaches.
The largest jump between two neighbouring samples, against the peak: a click or a cut anywhere in the attack.
How long the level takes to rise from 10 % to 90 % of its peak: the attack's speed as the ear feels it.
The loudest sample, against digital full scale. Near 0 dBFS risks clipping.
How loud the body of the sound is, weighted the way loudness meters are (K-weighting). The level two sounds are matched on before they are compared.
The peak over the body loudness: how much sharper the loudest moment is than the rest. A high crest is a spiky, punchy sound; a low one is dense or squashed.
How long, from the loudest moment, until the sound stays 20 dB quieter: how quickly it falls away at first.
How long until it stays 40 dB quieter: how long the ring lasts before it has dropped well down.
The time from 20 dB down to 40 dB down: how the tail behaves once the first thump is gone.
How fast the first stage of the decay falls, in dB a second.
How loud the late part of the ring still is, against the peak.
How fast the late ring falls, in dB a second. A slower late slope rings longer.
How loud the file's last 10 ms are: a file that ends while the sound still rings has been cut.
When the samples become exactly zero: a gate, a fade or an edit, not the sound dying naturally.
The pitch the drum settles to: the lowest steady resonance within 12 dB of the strongest. What you would tune a drum to.
The strongest resonance of the ring, which is not always the rest pitch.
How long the rest pitch takes to fall 60 dB: how long the drum's note rings.
The strongest resonance during the attack, before the pitch settles.
How far the attack's pitch sits above or below the rest pitch, in cents: a drum whose pitch drops after the strike reads positive.
How far the rest pitch's line sits here from where it settles, in cents: a tom's or a kick's downward glide.
How clearly a pitch stands out of the spectrum (its peak over the median): high for a tuned tom, low for a noisy snare.
Energy near the pitch against energy above it: body against brightness.
Table: every resonance found in one time window — its frequency, level and decay. The drum's modes, window by window.
How bright the sound is in a window: where its energy sits on average (the spectral centroid).
Where the energy sits as the ear weights it (A-weighted median frequency): half the heard energy is above, half below.
The strongest resonance in the smoothed spectrum: a body, a shell or a filter peak.
How sharp that resonance is: its frequency over its width. High Q rings narrowly; low Q is broad.
How loud a window is against the sound's peak.
One octave's level against the whole sound at that moment: the spectral shape, octave by octave.
How much of the energy sits in steady, predictable lines rather than noise: tone against hiss.
What the spectral peaks are between 20 and 200 ms: clean lines (1), resonant noise (0) or a mix (0.5).
The share of the sound between 1.6 and 6.4 kHz: a snare's springs rattling.
Buzz above 1.6 kHz against body below 400 Hz: how much of the snare is wires against drum.
How loud the wire band still is late in the sound: wires that keep sizzling after the drum.
How much the wire band's level swings from millisecond to millisecond: a smooth sizzle against a spitty one. One render's draw: compare several.
Whether the wire bursts cluster in time: a rattle that comes in clumps. One render's draw: compare several.
How peaky the sound's fine detail is (kurtosis): sharp slaps of the wires against a smooth sizzle.
The same slap sharpness as the typical 2 ms crest: its peaks against its average.
How strongly the wire level is modulated: the buzz's own rhythm, which reads as slapping when it is too pronounced.
Whether the envelope repeats between 1 and 20 ms: a rattle with a regular beat.
How much the ring's level wobbles (envelope modulation above 15 Hz): an unsteady, warbling ring. One render's draw.
How wide the ring's line is 3 dB down: a steady line is narrow, a wobbling or beating one wide.
How wide the ring's line is 10 dB down: the same, lower on its skirts.
How much of the sound is the ring, against the rest.
How strongly the envelope moves between 15 and 300 Hz, as a share: a buzzy or rough sound. One render's draw.
Table: pairs of resonances close enough to beat at their difference — the wah-wah of two nearly equal modes.
How much high-frequency energy the first 2 ms hold against the next 10: a click at the onset.
How loud the quietest 50 ms are: the recording's noise floor.
How loud the file is before the sound starts: noise, bleed or a previous note.
Mains hum at 50 Hz and its harmonics: the recording chain, not the sound.
Mains hum at 60 Hz and its harmonics: the recording chain, not the sound.
How loud the sound is at its loudest, in sone, from a model of hearing (ECMA-418-2). Twice the sone is twice as loud to the ear.
When the sound is loudest to the ear, from the onset.
How long the sound stays at least half as loud as its peak, to the ear: its heard length.
How loud a window sounds, in sone.
How sharp a window sounds (acum): its high-frequency weight as the ear hears it. Sharp is bright and cutting.
How tonal a window sounds (tu): how much the ear hears pitch rather than noise.
How rough a window sounds (asper): fast beating heard as grit.
Table: loudness, sharpness, tonality and roughness through the sound, from the onset.
Boominess: how much of the loudness sits under 280 Hz.
Brightness: the energy above 3 kHz against the whole.
Where the bright energy above 3 kHz sits: higher is airier.
Depth: the energy between 30 and 200 Hz against the whole.
Where that deep energy sits: lower is deeper.
Warmth: the energy from 150 to 600 Hz against 600 Hz to 6 kHz.
Hardness: how steep the attack's rise is, as the time a rise that steep would take to reach the peak. Shorter is harder.
Hardness as brightness: where the first 10 ms's energy sits.
The note's fundamental frequency: its lowest strong partial, the one a string's or a bar's pitch is named from.
How far the note sits from equal temperament (A = 440 Hz), in cents.
The pitch the ear takes, formed from several partials: for a bell it can differ from the fundamental.
How far the heard (virtual) pitch sits from equal temperament, in cents.
How long the fundamental takes to fall 60 dB: how long the note rings.
How the decay changes with frequency: 0 means every partial dies together; negative means the high partials die faster, as in most real materials.
How the partials' levels fall with frequency at the strike, in dB an octave: dark notes tilt steeply, bright ones gently.
Table: every partial within 40 dB of the strongest — frequency, ratio to the fundamental, level and decay.
How far the partials sit from the nearest ideal object (a string, a bar, a membrane…): near zero means the note behaves like that object.
How far apart the two lines of a split fundamental are: two strings of a unison, or a bar and its resonator, a little out of tune.
How much slower the fundamental's second decay stage is than its first: a piano's long aftersound.
When a damper comes down on the note (note-off), from the onset.
How fast the note dies once damped.
How fast the fundamental's level swings: two polarisations of a string, or a bar and its resonator, beating.
How far the fundamental's level swings while it beats.
How many onsets start the note: one for a pluck, several for a strum.
The time from the first onset to the last: how slow the strum is.
How many harmonics of a series were found: a string or a tube.
How far a stiff string's overtones are stretched above whole multiples (B): a piano's bass has more than a guitar's.
The second harmonic against the first.
The third harmonic against the first.
Even harmonics against odd: a clarinet is odd-heavy, a pickup's nonlinearity adds even.
How many harmonics among the first twelve are missing or sunk under the series: the holes a pluck point or a closed tube leaves.
Where the string was plucked or struck, as a share of its length: near the end is bright, near the middle hollow.
A partial's level at the strike against the fundamental, when two notes are compared partial by partial.
A partial's decay time, when two notes are compared partial by partial.
A partial's ratio to the fundamental against the reference's, in cents, when two notes are compared partial by partial.
How long a held note takes before its pitch holds.
How far the held pitch wanders, in cents a second.
How fast the vibrato swings.
How far the vibrato swings, in cents.
The pitch's small restlessness once the drift and the vibrato are taken out.
How fast the level swings (tremolo).
How far the level swings, in dB.
The harmonics against the noise between them: a clean tone against a breathy or scratchy one.
How long the note is held steady.
How strongly the ear hears slow level or pitch swings (fluctuation strength, vacil): a vibrato or tremolo's heard size.
Energy off the harmonic grid against on it: partials a digital oscillator folds back from above half the sample rate into the heard band.
Whether the worst aliasing is heard: above zero it pokes out of the harmonics' masking, below zero it hides under them.
A line off the harmonic series: a filter singing on its own, or a second oscillator.
Harmonic distortion: orders 2 to 10 against the fundamental.
Where a peak stands on the harmonic series: a resonant filter's cutoff.
How far that peak stands over the series' line: the filter's resonance.
A constant offset in the signal: no sound, but it moves the waveform off centre.
The envelope's attack time.
The envelope's decay time to the sustain level.
The sustain level against the peak.
The release: from note-off until 60 dB down.
A click at note-on, over the held sound's own texture.
A click at note-off, over the held sound's own texture.
The rate of a stepped control in the envelope: parameter changes heard as zipper noise.
How loud the zipper's sidebands are against the envelope.
How fast a detuned unison beats.
How far apart a unison's voices are tuned.
Table: every harmonic's level against the fundamental.
How linear and steady the device is under noise: 1 means a filter or delay, lower means it is moving or distorting (a chorus reads about 0.5).
When the response's first arrival peaks: the device's delay.
The response's gain at 1 kHz.
Where the frequency response peaks.
How far that peak stands over the passband.
How sharp that peak is.
The low edge: where the response is 3 dB under its passband.
The high edge: where the response is 3 dB under its passband.
Table: the frequency response at third-octave centres.
Table: discrete echoes standing out of the response.
The first echo.
The delay time: the spacing of evenly spaced repeats.
Table: the evenly spaced repeats.
Each repeat's level against the one before: the feedback setting.
How each repeat changes its highs against its lows: a darkening tape or bucket-brigade echo.
The reverberation time: how long the space takes to fall 60 dB, judged from its fall between −5 and −35 dB.
The early decay time: how fast the first 10 dB fall, scaled to 60 dB. It follows how reverberant a space sounds more closely than the T30.
The gap between the direct sound and the first reflection.
The direct sound against the reverberation: close or far.
When the echoes become dense enough to sound like a smooth tail.
How alike the two ears' late reverberation is: low is wide and enveloping.
How far the space analysis trusts itself, from 0 to 1.
The effect's gain at the test tone.
Total harmonic distortion: harmonics 2 to 10 against the tone.
The second harmonic against the tone: warm, even distortion.
The third harmonic against the tone: harder, odd distortion.
A constant offset the effect adds.
Table: every harmonic's level against the tone.
How fast the tone's pitch wobbles: a chorus, a vibrato, or tape flutter.
How far the tone's pitch wobbles.
How fast the tone's level wobbles: a tremolo.
How far the tone's level wobbles.
Second-order intermodulation: new tones at the sum and difference of two input tones.
Third-order intermodulation: new tones close beside the input tones, the most audible kind.
Intermodulation distortion measured the SMPTE way.
A compressor's threshold: the level where its gain starts to fall.
A compressor's ratio: input dB per output dB above the threshold.
The gain below the threshold.
A compressor's attack: how fast its gain moves after a step up.
A compressor's release: how fast its gain recovers after a step down.
Table: the static curve, output level against input level.
The effect's own noise with silence in.
How fast the level grows or dies on silence: a feedback loop running away reads positive.
A steady line on silence: self-oscillation or hum.
How loud that line is.
The effect's typical gain during a burst.
The first burst's gain against the rest: an effect that changes after it wakes.
How long the effect keeps sounding after a burst ends, until it stays 40 dB under it.
How fast a moving delay sweeps: a chorus or flanger's rate.
How far the delay sweeps.
The swept delay's mean: short for a flanger, longer for a chorus.
The sweep's shape: its third harmonic against its first. A triangle sweep reads about −19 dB, a sine far lower.
The right channel's sweep against the left's: how the chorus spreads.
How alike left and right are: 1 is mono, 0 unrelated, −1 opposed.
The side against the mid: how wide the sound is.
Left against right: how the sound leans.
How much of the left input reaches the right output, against the left output.
How much of the right input reaches the left output, against the right output.
The left input's paths against the right input's: whether the two inputs are treated alike.
Table: every input-to-output path of a true-stereo device, against the strongest.
Table: the readings of several responses against the setting that changed between them.
The sound's level over time, against its loudest moment: the line its attack, decay and ring are read from.
The whole sound's level against frequency, against its loudest band: where its energy sits.
The sound's level over time and frequency at once, in bands spaced as the ear spaces them: which parts ring, which die, and when.
